summary.text: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 that is not a product of two smaller natural numbers.
Primes are central in number theory because every natural number greater than 1 is either prime or a product of primes, unique up to their order.
There are infinitely many primes, no known simple formula separates them from composites, and public-key cryptography relies on how hard it is to factor large numbers.

facts.label: Divisor test
facts.value: A prime has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself

facts.label: Unsolved questions
facts.value: Goldbach's conjecture and the twin prime conjecture

items.prompt: A friend says 1 should count as prime because no smaller numbers multiply to make it. Why is 1 left out?

options.label: It is even, and primes must be odd
It is too small to be written as a product
A prime has exactly two divisors, and 1 has only one
It is a multiple of every other number

items.explain: Primes are the numbers with exactly two positive divisors, 1 and themselves, and 1 has only one divisor.

items.prompt: A number larger than 5 ends in the digit 5. Could it be prime?

options.label: Yes, any odd number could be
Yes, as long as it is over 100
Only if its other digits are all odd
No, it is divisible by 5

items.explain: Primes larger than 5 end in 1, 3, 7 or 9; numbers ending in 0 or 5 are divisible by 5, so they are composite.

items.prompt: Why can a large even number such as 1,000 never be prime?

options.label: It is the product of 2 and a smaller number
Primes stop appearing past a few hundred
It has far too many digits to be prime
It is always divisible by 3 as well

items.explain: Any even number above 2 can be written as 2 × n/2, so it is a product of smaller numbers.

items.prompt: You can arrange a pile of dots into a rectangle at least two dots wide and two high. What does that tell you about the count?

options.label: It is a prime number
It is a composite number
It is exactly 1
It must be even

items.explain: A number is prime only if its dots cannot be arranged in such a grid, so a count that can be is composite.

items.prompt: Why do number theorists treat primes as the building blocks of whole numbers?

options.label: Every even number is a sum of two primes
Primes appear at perfectly regular intervals
Every number over 1 is a prime or a product of primes, in one way
Primes are the only numbers with a divisor

items.explain: The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says each natural number above 1 is prime or factors into primes, uniquely up to order. The sum-of-two-primes claim is Goldbach's conjecture, still unsolved.

items.prompt: As numbers get larger, how does the chance that a randomly chosen one is prime change?

options.label: It stays the same at every size
It rises, since bigger numbers have more room
It falls, tied inversely to the number of digits
It drops to zero beyond a certain size

items.explain: The prime number theorem says the chance for a large number is inversely proportional to its number of digits, so primes thin out.
